items.title: CM0 – A new Raspberry Pi you can't buy
items.raw_content: This little postage stamp is actually a full Raspberry Pi Zero 2, complete with eMMC storage and WiFi. But you can't get one. Well, not unless you buy the CM0NANO development board from EDAtec, or you live in China. This little guy doesn't have an HDMI port, Ethernet, or even USB. It's a special version of the 'Compute Module' line of boards. Little Raspberry Pi 'System on Modules' (SoMs), they're called.
items.title_zh: CM0——一款买不到的新树莓派
items.summary: A postage-stamp-sized board that is effectively a full Raspberry Pi Zero 2 with eMMC storage and WiFi, but it is not available for general purchase — only through EDAtec's CM0NANO development board or in China. The Compute Module variant has no HDMI, Ethernet or USB.

items.title: CRISPR fungus: Protein-packed, sustainable, and tastes like meat
items.raw_content: Researchers have successfully used CRISPR gene editing technology to create a fungi strain that is highly efficient, more nutritious, and significantly more sustainable than its natural counterpart. The fungus Fusarium venenatum already stands out for its meat-like flavor and texture, leading to its approval for food use in several countries. This breakthrough, published in the journal Trends in Biotechnology, addresses the need for better, more environmentally friendly alternatives to conventional animal agriculture, which accounts for about 14% of global greenhouse gas emissions.
items.title_zh: CRISPR 真菌：富含蛋白、可持续，味道像肉
items.summary: Researchers used CRISPR gene editing to create a strain of the fungus Fusarium venenatum that is more efficient, nutritious and sustainable than its natural counterpart, according to a study in Trends in Biotechnology. The fungus is already approved for food in several countries and has a meat-like flavor and texture.

items.title: Rats Play DOOM
items.raw_content: We built a complete VR setup from scratch to let rats play DOOM. The system includes a motion-tracked treadmill ball, a panoramic headset, an input trigger, and a reward circuit. All hardware and software components are open sourced, including 3D-printable designs, circuit diagrams, firmware, and control software. The first version (v1) was built in New York by Viktor , who trained rats to walk through a corridor in DOOM using a simpler rig. That version was featured on Vice and PC Gamer. After moving back home, the project was paused. Public interest reignited development, leading to v2, a more advanced and modular version built in collaboration with electrical engineer Sándor Makra . Akos Blaschek later assisted significantly in documenting the project for open-sourcing, aiming to enable others to replicate and build upon this work. items.summary: The project built a complete VR setup from scratch to let rats play DOOM, including a motion-tracked treadmill ball, a panoramic headset, an input trigger and a reward circuit, with all hardware and software open sourced.

items.title: GNU Unifont
items.raw_content: GNU Unifont is a Unicode-based dual-width monochrome font, with glyphs in a grid of 8 or 16 pixels wide by 16 pixels tall. Currently, the main format is OpenType, which provides scalable glyphs (see an OpenType sample at left). The original intent of Unifont was to offer a simple font format with wide Unicode coverage to render something meaningful for each Unicode code point, rather than a blank box (“tofu”) for missing glyphs. This simple format has allowed many, many volunteers to contribute thousands of glyphs. This page contains the latest release of GNU Unifont, with glyphs for every printable code point in the Unicode Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP). The BMP occupies the first 65,536 code points of the Unicode space, denoted as U+0000..U+FFFF. There is also growing coverage of the Supplementary Multilingual Plane (SMP), in the range U+010000..U+01FFFF, of Michael Everson's ConScrip
items.title_zh: GNU Unifont
items.summary: GNU Unifont is a Unicode-based dual-width monochrome font with glyphs on an 8- or 16-pixel-wide by 16-pixel-tall grid, now distributed mainly as scalable OpenType. It aims to cover every printable code point in the Unicode Basic Multilingual Plane so missing characters do not render as blank boxes, with growing coverage of the Supplementary Multilingual Plane.
